## **Module 5: Cryosphere Processes on Earth Relevant to Ocean Worlds**

**Authors**

**Don Blankenship, Terry Hurford, Natalie Wolfenbarger, Justin Lawrence, Marggy Chiviri**

Europa, one of Jupiter's four Galilean moons, stands out in the quest to find extraterrestrial life within our solar system. Europa is believed to harbor a global salty ocean beneath an icy crust that is estimated to be kilometers to tens of kilometers thick. This module focuses on processes hypothesized for Europa's ice shell, drawing parallels to processes found in Earth's ice-covered regions. In preparation for testing these hypotheses, cryospheric processes are discussed through the lens of the Radar for Europa Assessment and Sounding: Ocean to Near Surface (REASON) instrument on NASA's Europa Clipper mission. Building on a rich heritage of ice-penetrating radar investigations on Earth, REASON is uniquely capable of directly probing Europa's ice shell to study cryospheric processes that govern material exchange between the surface, ice shell, and ocean.

In this module, we will explore the foundational concepts of Europa's geological features, the key scientific goals of the REASON instrument on the Europa Clipper mission, and the measurement techniques REASON will employ to understand this icy world. Detailed investigations into the distribution of subsurface water distribution, the ice-ocean interface, and material exchange processes will be discussed, highlighting the use of terrestrial analog studies to interpret data. By addressing the barriers and knowledge gaps in interpreting ice-penetrating radar data, this module aims to bridge the gap between Earth's cryosphere and the icy moons of our solar system, paving the way for future research and exploration.

## **Level 1: Foundational Concepts and Basic Information**

### **1.1 Overview of Europa and Its Importance**

Europa is one of Jupiter's four Galilean moons (Fig. 1), discovered along with Io, Ganymede, and Callisto in 1610. It wasn't until almost 400 years later that we were able to send a dedicated spacecraft mission to study these moons. Through the Galileo mission, which operated from 1995 to 2003, we gained an unprecedented view of these moons (Fig. 1), revealing their unique characteristics and potential for further exploration [(Showman & Malhotra, 1999)](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.286.5437.77). Among these moons, Europa stood out for its young surface (~100 Ma) and compelling evidence of a global subsurface ocean, making it a prime candidate in the search for life beyond Earth within our solar system [(Pappalardo et al., 2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-024-01070-5).

![][image1]

**Figure 1.1** Jupiter's four Galilean satellites were studied by NASA's Galileo mission, which explored the Jovian system from 1995 to 2003 (Credit: NASA/JPL).

Estimates of the thickness of Europa's icy crust range from kilometers to tens of kilometers thick [(Billings & Kattenhorn, 2005)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0019103505001211). The crust is composed of ice Ih (hexagonal crystals), the dominant form of ice on Earth, but also contains non-ice impurities including salts entrained through freezing of the underlying ocean and acids generated through radiolytic processing of surface materials [(Becker et al., 2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-024-01069-y). Europa's saline subsurface ocean is estimated to be ~100 km thick and lies beneath an icy crust [(Roberts et al., 2023)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-023-00990-y). The ocean is thought to be sustained by tidal heating driven by Jupiter's strong gravitational field [(Ross & Schubert, 1987)](https://www.nature.com/articles/325133a0). The subsurface ocean is in contact with a rocky seafloor (Fig. 2), which is important for potential chemical interactions that could support life [(Vance et al., 2023)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-023-01025-2).

![A structure of the planet Description automatically generated][image2]

**Figure 1.2** Europa is a rocky moon with an outer layer of H<sub>2</sub>O (Credit: NASA/JPL).

Regions of disrupted ice, which appear jumbled and chaotic (Fig. 3), may form through interaction with liquid water pockets that form within the ice shell, causing the surface ice above to collapse, shift, and eventually refreeze [(Collins & Nimmo, 2009)](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Chaotic-Terrain-on-Europa-Collins-Nimmo/7f17d4018698e422d9922c55949b3c425d089a67). Extensive plains marked by ridges (Fig. 3), indicative of tectonic activity where the surface ice has been fractured and pulled apart, possibly by the tidal forces from Jupiter [(Prockter & Patterson, 2009)](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Morphology-and-Evolution-of-Europa%27s-Ridges-and-Prockter-Patterson/996f646cfc43227acc047d66936d0886a161f3b3). Europa's surface is constantly reshaped by these processes and lacks the heavily cratered topography of older surfaces (like our own Moon's) indicating that Europa is geologically active with ongoing surface renewal [(Daubar et al., 2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-023-01036-z).

![][image3]

**Figure 1.3** Europa's surface is characterized by dynamic and bizarre geology, such as ridged plains and chaos terrain (Credit: NASA/JPL).

### **1.2 REASON on Europa Clipper**

The REASON ice-penetrating radar instrument on NASA's Europa Clipper mission will use VHF (60 MHz) and HF (9 MHz) frequencies to probe Europa's ice shell from the exosphere to the ice-ocean interface (Fig. 4). REASON operates by transmitting radio waves into the ice shell and recording energy reflected from interfaces defined by contrasts in dielectric properties [(Blankenship et al., 2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-024-01072-3).

![][image4]

**Figure 1.4** The REASON instrument will use VHF (60 MHz) and HF (9 MHz) frequencies to probe Europa's ice shell from the exosphere to the ice-ocean interface (Modified from Blankenship et al. [(2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-024-01072-3).

The REASON instrument will employ multiple measurement techniques including: Sounding for subsurface structure, Altimetry for relative surface elevation, Interferometry for clutter discrimination, Reflectometry for near-surface roughness, porosity, and composition, Plasma Characterization to estimate total electron content and identify active plumes, and Ranging for detecting changes in surface elevation as a function of time (Fig. 5). Depending on the properties of the ice shell that influence radar penetration depths (like ice temperature and salinity), REASON may even be able to image the ice-ocean interface and interactions with the ocean at the base of the ice shell [(Kalousová et al., 2017)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/2016JE005110).

![][image5]

**Figure 1.5** REASON will employ multiple measurement techniques, including Sounding, Altimetry, Interferometry, Reflectometry, Plasma Characterization, and Ranging (Modified from Blankenship et al. [(2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-024-01072-3).

## **Level 2: Detailed Exploration and Advanced Understanding**

### **2.1 Scientific Investigations**


#### **_2.1.1 Shallow Water_**

REASON will use Sounding, Reflectometry, and Altimetry measurements to characterize the distribution of any shallow subsurface water [(Blankenship et al., 2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-024-01072-3). Radar sounding measurements can detect subglacial water bodies [(e.g., Young et al., 2016)](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsta/article/374/2059/20140297/115084/The-distribution-of-basal-water-between-Antarctic), including perched water bodies that may be trapped within the ice [(Culha et al., 2019)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0019103518304937). Reflectometry measurements will help identify areas where brines have been introduced near the surface [(e.g., Grima et al., 2016)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/2016GL069524), such as those hypothesized to be linked to chaos terrain formation [(Schmidt et al., 2011)](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10608). Altimetry measurements will be used to evaluate whether interfaces detected by radar are in hydrostatic equilibrium, and are therefore consistent with the presence of liquid water [(e.g., Ewert et al., 2012](https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/191/2/557/642475); [Vaughan et al., 2007](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2007GL030769)).

![A close-up of a water investigation Description automatically generated][image6]

**Figure 2.1** REASON will use Sounding, Reflectometry, and Altimetry measurements to characterize the distribution of any shallow subsurface water (Credit: NASA, UTIG).

#### **_2.1.2 Ocean Search_**

REASON will use Sounding and Altimetry measurements to search for an ice-ocean interface and characterize the ice shell's global thermophysical structure [(Blankenship et al., 2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-024-01072-3). Through searching for an ice-ocean interface, we can confirm the existence of a global subsurface ocean and determine the thickness of the ice shell. This will involve resolving whether the ice shell is thin (i.e., only a few kilometers) or thick (tens of kilometers) (Fig. 7). Understanding how variable the ice shell thickness is, or the depth of the ice-ocean interface, can help us understand how ocean circulation and ice shell freezing and melting processes interact [(Soderlund et al., 2020)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-020-00706-6). Depending on the ice thickness, temperature, and composition, the ice shell may undergo solid-state convection [(Barr & Showman, 2009)](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Heat-Transfer-in-Europa%27s-Icy-Shell-Barr-Showman/2c9855fc5640771306a8c2751c374fa2a6e3cf93). We can use radar sounding observations of attenuation rate to look for temperature signatures that would indicate ice convection [(Kalousová et al., 2017)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/2016JE005110).

![][image7]

**Figure 2.2** REASON will use Sounding and Altimetry measurements to search for an ice-ocean interface and characterize the ice shell's global thermophysical structure (Credit: NASA/JPL, UTIG).

#### **_2.1.3 Material Exchange_**

REASON will use Sounding and Altimetry measurements to investigate the processes governing material exchange among the ocean, ice shell, surface, and exosphere (Fig. 8). By comparing the processes governing ice-ocean material exchange on Earth, such as those seen in subglacial Lake Vostok in Antarctica [(e.g., MacGregor et al., 2009)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0012821X09001629), researchers can infer similar processes on Europa [(Blankenship et al., 2009)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?spbjG4). This helps in understanding how materials like salts and nutrients - and possibly life - could move between the ocean, ice shell, and surface on Europa.

![][image8]

**Figure 2.3** REASON will use Sounding and Altimetry measurements to investigate the processes governing material exchange among the ocean, ice shell, surface, and exosphere (Credit: UTIG; Lake Vostok radargram modified from Blankenship et al. [(2009)](https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/epsc2009/epsc2009-636.pdf).

#### **_2.1.4 Gravitational Tides_**

REASON will use Ranging measurements to constrain Europa's radial tidal deformations (Fig. 9). Measuring the amplitude of Europa's tides can provide clues about the internal structure of the moon, such as the presence of an ocean [(Wahr et al., 2006)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2006JE002729).

![A diagram of planets in outer space Description automatically generated][image9]

**Figure 2.4** REASON will use Ranging measurements to constrain Europa's radial tidal deformations (Credit: NASA/JPL).

### **2.2 Heritage from Earth and Mars**

Although REASON will be the first ice-penetrating radar to explore the outer solar system, it builds upon a rich heritage of radar investigations on Earth, the Moon, and Mars (Fig. 10, 11). Radar sounding of Mars' polar caps has been successful at multiple frequencies ([Croci et al., 2011](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5713217); [Orosei et al., 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0032063314002153)), demonstrating the capability of ice-penetrating radars as components of spacecraft payloads to probe and characterize unknown subsurface environments of other worlds.

![][image10]

**Figure 2.5** Radar investigations of Mars with MARSIS and SHARAD provide a scientific and technological foundation for REASON [(Blankenship et al., 2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-024-01072-3).

Airborne radar sounding of floating ice on Earth (e.g., ice shelves, icebergs, subglacial lakes) can be used to inform and validate the interpretations of radar data collected at Europa (Fig. 11).

![A comparison of a scale of the earth Description automatically generated with medium confidence][image11]

**Figure 2.6** Radar investigations of Earth's cryosphere can inform interpretation of data collected by REASON at Europa [(Blankenship et al., 2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-024-01072-3).

### **2.3 Earth and Mars Analogs for REASON Measurements**

Radar investigations of Earth and Mars can be used as analogs for Europa to validate REASON measurement techniques (Fig. 12). Altimetry and Sounding measurements over iceberg B15 demonstrate how shallow subsurface structure at Europa could be characterized through detection of multiple interfaces ([Peters et al., 2007](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/4063308/)). Reflectometry measurements over McMurdo Ice Shelf, Antarctica, demonstrate how the roughness, porosity, and composition of Europa's near-surface could be constrained [(Grima et al., 2016)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/2016GL069524). Techniques for estimating the total electron content of Mars' ionosphere can be applied to Europa to identify anomalies that could be associated with plume activity ([Grima et al., 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0032063315002470); [Scanlan et al., 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0032063319300820)).

![A close-up of a diagram Description automatically generated][image12]

Young et al., 2011](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10114), [2017](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/11/1897/2017/)), focus on ice characterization using ice-penetrating radar in Antarctica and the Arctic. Techniques include using VHF antennas, helicopter radar, and gravity surveys to gather detailed ice data , which can be applied to understanding Europa's ice shell.

## **Level 3: Technical Insights and Case Studies**

### **3.1 Europa's Ice Shell and Lessons from Ocean-Ice Interactions on Earth**

Europa's ice shell likely formed through freezing of the underlying ocean. Ice formed through the freezing of saline water has a non-zero bulk salinity due to the interstitial trapping of brine (Fig. 14). Understanding the formation and properties of sea ice on Earth, including data from ice cores, helps in modeling similar processes on Europa ([Buffo et al., 2020](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2020JE006394); [Wolfenbarger, et al., 2022](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/ast.2021.0044)).

![][image14]

**Figure 3.1** Ice which forms through the freezing of saline water has a non-zero bulk ice salinity due to the interstitial trapping of brine (Modified from Buffo et al. [(2020)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2020JE006394) (left) and Wolfenbarger et al. [(2022)](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/ast.2021.0044) (right)).

Ice cores collected from beneath Antarctic ice shelves show distinct salinity profiles associated with different mechanisms of ice formation, which can be used to develop hypotheses for ice-ocean exchange processes and their effect on the properties of Europa's ice shell (Fig. 15).

**Marine Ice:** Marine ice forms through the accumulation and consolidation of frazil ice crystals beneath an ice shelf ([Wolfenbarger et al., 2022](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/ast.2021.0044)). Frazil ice crystals form via an "ice pump" mechanism ([Lewis & Perkin, 1986](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/JC091iC10p11756)), where melting beneath an ice shelf generates fresh, buoyant meltwater which rises to shallower depths forming a plume of supercooled water that promotes the crystallization of frazil ice ([Lawrence et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023JE008036)). The formation of marine ice at Europa is hypothesized to occur where there are gradients in ice shell thickness ([Lawrence et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023JE008036); [Soderlund et al., 2013](https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo2021); [Wolfenbarger et al., 2022](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/ast.2021.0044)).

**Sub-Ice-Shelf Congelation Ice:** Sub-ice-shelf congelation ice refers to slow-growing "sea ice" found beneath ice shelves, where seawater freezes directly to the ice-ocean interface forming columnar crystals ([Wolfenbarger et al., 2022](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/ast.2021.0044)). If Europa's ice shell formed through freezing of an ocean, the ice is likely to be an analog of Earth's sub-ice-shelf congelation ice ([Buffo et al., 2020](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2020JE006394); [Wolfenbarger et al., 2022](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/ast.2021.0044)).

![][image15]

**Figure 3.2** Two distinct mechanisms of ice formation operate beneath Earth's ice shelves, serving as analogs for processes that may take place at Europa's ice-ocean interface (Modified from Wolfenbarger et al. [(2022)](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/ast.2021.0044) (top), Lawrence et al. [(2024)](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023JE008036) (bottom left) and Zotikov et al. [(1980)](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.207.4438.1463) (bottom right)).

Surveys over Earth ice shelves, including Filchner-Ronne and Amery Ice Shelf, show that marine ice can be detected using radar ([Fricker et al., 2001](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1029/2000GL012461); [Lambrecht et al., 2007](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/antarctic-science/article/abs/new-ice-thickness-maps-of-filchnerronne-ice-shelf-antarctica-with-specific-focus-on-grounding-lines-and-marine-ice/23C0FD97CC5840174727F3989B8E94DF); [Sandhäger et al., 2004](https://www.bas.ac.uk/data/our-data/publication/meteoric-marine-and-total-ice-thickness-maps-of-filchner-ronne-schelfeis-antarctica/); [Thyssen, 1988](https://articles.researchsolutions.com/special-aspects-of-the-central-part-of-filchner-ronne-ice-shelf-antarctica/doi/10.3189/s0260305500006509)). The radar reflection from the meteoric-marine interface is caused by the higher electrical conductivity of the marine ice layer. A key question is whether accretion ice within Europa's ice shell will have distinct radiometric signatures that can be detected by radar.

![A diagram of a sea shell Description automatically generated with medium confidence][image16]

**Figure 3.3** Surveys over Earth ice shelves show that marine ice can be detected using ice-penetrating radar (Modified from Sandhäger et al. [(2004)](https://www.bas.ac.uk/data/our-data/publication/meteoric-marine-and-total-ice-thickness-maps-of-filchner-ronne-schelfeis-antarctica/) (left) and Thyssen [(1988)](https://articles.researchsolutions.com/special-aspects-of-the-central-part-of-filchner-ronne-ice-shelf-antarctica/doi/10.3189/s0260305500006509) (right)).

### **3.2 Surface Features**

The formation of Europa's surface features are thought to be controlled by cryospheric processes occurring in the subsurface.

#### **_3.2.1 Chaos_**

Hypotheses suggest that chaos terrains on Europa are formed through interactions between the subsurface ocean and/or the ice shell, causing melting and refreezing (Fig. 17).

![][image17]

**Figure 3.4** Many of the hypotheses proposed for the formation of chaos terrain involved the presence of subsurface water (Modified from Collins & Nimmo [(2009)](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Chaotic-Terrain-on-Europa-Collins-Nimmo/7f17d4018698e422d9922c55949b3c425d089a67).

Earth analogs, such as subglacial volcanic lakes in Iceland and brine-infiltrated Antarctic ice shelves, guided the development of a lens-collapse hypothesis by providing insights into the interactions between water and ice under pressure [(Schmidt et al., 2011)](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10608). Variations in surface topography associated with Conamara Chaos and Thera Macula support the lens-collapse model as most compatible with the formation of these features (Fig. 18).

![A collage of images of different types of light Description automatically generated][image18]

**Figure 3.5** A lens-collapse model of chaos formation is most compatible with the topography over chaos features (Modified from Schmidt et al. [(2011)](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10608).

#### **_3.2.2 Double Ridges_**

Studies suggest that ridges on Europa could form through tectonic processes similar to those on Earth. Similar to chaos formation, the presence of liquid water is common to many of the ridge formation hypotheses (Fig. 19).

![A collage of images of a frozen ice Description automatically generated][image19]

**Figure 3.6** The presence of liquid water is common to many of the proposed hypotheses for ridge formation (Modified from Dombard et al. [(2013)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0019103512004757)).

The presence of flanking fractures associated with double ridge features supports the hypothesis of subsurface liquid water sills (Fig. 20).

![A collage of images of a structure Description automatically generated][image20]

**Figure 3.7** The presence of liquid water is common to many of the proposed hypotheses for ridge formation (Modified from Dombard et al. ([2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0019103512004757)).

The recent discovery of a double ridge in Greenland's ice sheet supports that melting and refreezing within a porous, fractured ice shell could be responsible for the formation of Europa's double ridges (Fig. 21).

![A collage of images of a structure Description automatically generated][image21]

**Figure 3.8** A double ridge feature discovered in Greenland was used as an analog to study the process of double ridge formation at Europa (Modified from Culberg et al. ([2022](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-29458-3)))

#### **_3.2.3 Bands_**

Bands are hypothesized to be locations where subduction-like processes occur on Europa, where a cold dense layer of surface ice is subsumed into a warmer, less dense layer of the ice shell (Fig. 22). This process is similar to tectonic activity on Earth and could have significant implications for Europa's geological activity and processes of surface-ice-ocean exchange.

![][image22]

**Figure 3.9** Evidence for a subduction-like process suggests a process analogous to Earth's plate tectonics may operate at Europa (Modified from Kattenhorn & Prockter ([2014](https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo2245))).

### **3.3 Salt Layers**

Many of the hypotheses proposed to explain the formation of Europa's surface features involve the presence of liquid water within the ice shell. Water reservoirs within the ice shell-whether generated through melting of the ice shell or through injection of ocean-water through basal fractures-will begin to freeze as they thermally equilibrate with the surrounding ice. As these reservoirs freeze, they undergo a process known as cryoconcentration where the water salinity increases as the volume of liquid water decreases upon ice formation (Fig. 23). The freezing process ultimately concludes with the formation of a layer (or layers) composed of a mixture of ice and hydrated salt minerals, known as salt layers ([Chivers et al., 2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/PSJ/acea75); [Chivers et al., 2021](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2020JE006692); [Naseem et al., 2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/PSJ/ace5a2); [Wolfenbarger et al., 2023](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2024GL109144)). These salt layers represent radar-detectable structures within the ice shell that can serve as evidence of sites where liquid water was once present ([Wolfenbarger et al., 2023](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2024GL109144)). Through radar characterization of these salt layers, it may be possible to distinguish whether these water reservoirs are sourced from ocean-injection or melting of the ice shell ([Wolfenbarger et al., 2023](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2024GL109144)).

![][image23]

**Figure 3.10** Hypothesized water bodies within Europa's ice shell will evolve into salt layers as they freeze (Modified from Wolfenbarger et al. [(2023)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2024GL109144)).

### **3.4 Brine Pockets**

Brine pockets are hypothesized to be present in the ice shell where temperatures exceed the eutectic temperature ([Wolfenbarger et al., 2022b](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022JE007305)). The interface associated with the transition from solid ice to ice containing brine has been referred to as a "eutectic interface" in the context of theoretical radar sounding studies applied to Europa ([Schroeder et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GL110635)). Because the temperature at which brine becomes thermodynamically stable is well-constrained with knowledge of the composition of non-ice impurities ([Wolfenbarger et al., 2022b](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022JE007305)), the detection of a eutectic interface could be used to constrain the thickness of the thermally conductive portion of Europa's ice shell ([Schroeder et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GL110635)). In addition to serving as a geophysical constraint, detection of brine in Europa's ice shell would be significant as a potential habitat to organisms that might inhabit the ice shell ([Wolfenbarger et al., 2022a](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022GL100586)). The meteoric-marine interface associated with the accretion of marine ice beneath ice shelves can be considered as an analog for a eutectic interface at Europa because it corresponds to a transition from solid ice to ice containing brine. Radar characterization of these meteoric-marine interfaces on Earth could guide the interpretation of eutectic interfaces detected at Europa (Fig. 24).

![A close up of a graph Description automatically generated][image24]

**Figure 3.11** Radar characterization of meteoric-marine interfaces beneath Earth's ice shelves could be used as an analog for radar characterization of eutectic interfaces within Europa's ice shell, representing potential habitats (Modified from Thyssen [(1988)](https://articles.researchsolutions.com/special-aspects-of-the-central-part-of-filchner-ronne-ice-shelf-antarctica/doi/10.3189/s0260305500006509) (left) and Wolfenbarger et al. ([2022a])(https://doi.org/10.1029/2022GL100586) (right)).

## **Synthesis and Future Directions**

Europa's icy shell and subsurface ocean represent a compelling target for understanding planetary processes and assessing the potential for extraterrestrial life. Drawing upon lessons from Earth's cryosphere and Mars' polar studies, this module has detailed the scientific goals and methodologies of the REASON ice-penetrating radar instrument on NASA's Europa Clipper mission. The cryospheric processes believed to shape Europa's ice shell, surface features, and subsurface structures are analyzed through the lens of terrestrial analogs. This module emphasizes the importance of analog studies, radar surveys, and advanced modeling efforts to bridge knowledge gaps between Earth-based cryospheric science and planetary exploration. Future research must address the challenges of interpreting radar data in cryospheric environments characterized by significant unknowns (ice shell thickness, temperature, composition). Priorities include developing robust remote sensing methodologies, refining ice shell models, and designing instruments for detecting life-signature analogs in extreme conditions. These efforts will rely on interdisciplinary collaboration, leveraging NSF-NASA partnerships, and expanding cryospheric research infrastructure.
